boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Proctor's Creek (Drewry's Bluff) record (May 12-16, 1864) in the Bermuda Hundred Campaign [May 1864]. Chester Station (VA051) precedes on May 10 and Ware Bottom Church (VA054) follows on May 20; Whiting's Petersburg column of May 16 is part of Beauregard's plan for this record. Army-wide returns, the campaign-wide casualty return and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 48,000 (US 30,000; CS 18,000), matching the frozen description; the live field reads 57,000 (US 39,000; CS 18,000) while its description keeps Butler's 30,000. Humphreys gives Beauregard not less than 17,000 enlisted infantry in three divisions at Drury's Bluff (Ransom about 5,400, Hoke about 7,000, Colquitt about 4,900) and Whiting not less than 4,600 muskets at Petersburg, reconstructs 22,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry by May 15, and says Butler's infantry before the intrenchments did not exceed the enemy's, with Ames's 5,000, Hinks's 5,000 and about 3,000 detached. Beauregard writes of the enemy's advantage in numbers.
claims.rationale: Mixed reconstructions of effective infantry, detached forces and commanders' comparisons; the Union and Confederate scopes differ. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Beauregard organized three divisions and a Petersburg column, withheld Ransom's advance at 10 a.m. when Ransom judged it unsafe, and blamed the incomplete result on the left wing's hesitation and Whiting's premature halt; his June 14 letter explains why he had first commended the left-wing commander. Humphreys says Davis approved the plan except Whiting's part, and that Butler ordered Gillmore to fall back at about 10 a.m. The frozen commanders are Major General Butler and General Beauregard; the live page gives Beauregard as Brigadier General.
claims.rationale: Direction and blame attributed as stated; Beauregard's criticism of his subordinates is an interested judgment. The live rank is not adopted. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 6,660 total; the live field reads 4,004 (US 3,004; CS 1,000). Humphreys gives Beauregard's report of 354 killed, 1,610 wounded and 220 missing (2,184) on May 16, and Badeau's Union figure for May 16 of 390 killed, 1,721 wounded and 1,390 missing (3,500), excluding earlier days, noting that Smith's and Gillmore's statements are incomplete. Beauregard claims 1,400 prisoners; his headquarters' casualty list is incomplete and garbled in OCR, and the prisoner list, also incomplete, appears to end with 43, 1,345 and 1,388 (column assignment not established in OCR).
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Several figures cover May 16 only; the prisoner count and the Union missing overlap and are not reconciled.

open_questions: Butler's May 12-18 telegrams (selected and read; not used here under the three-family ceiling), his May 5-31 casualty return (garbled), Smith's, Gillmore's, Weitzel's, Heckman's and Terry's reports, Ransom's, Hoke's, Whiting's and D. H. Hill's reports (Nos. 89-93, 102), Beauregard's May 16-17 telegrams (garbled) and the Richmond defences returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the Army of the Potomac's chief of staff, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; for this campaign it summarizes Smith's, Gillmore's and Weitzel's reports and quotes Beauregard's reports and telegrams, so it is not independent of the Beauregard family. Butler's telegrams and Hagood's, Barton's and Beauregard's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVI, Part 2, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
